q: What does dynamic programming require and produce in RL?
short: It requires a complete, accurate model of the MDP (transitions and rewards) and produces value functions and optimal policies by applying Bellman equations as iterative updates.
follow: Why is it rarely used directly?

q: Describe iterative policy evaluation.
short: Initialise V, then sweep all states applying V(s) ← Σₐ π(a|s) Σ p(s′, r|s, a)[r + γV(s′)] until the largest change Δ falls below θ; converges to v_π.

q: Write the value iteration update.
short: V(s) ← maxₐ Σ_{s′,r} p(s′, r|s, a)[r + γV(s′)], repeated until Δ < θ; then π(s) = argmaxₐ of the same expression.

q: Race car, γ = 0.9, V₀ = 0. Compute V₁ and V₂.
example: Fast wins in Cool already at sweep 2.

q: What is policy iteration?
short: Repeat: evaluate the current policy fully (v_π), then improve it by acting greedily with respect to v_π; stop when the policy no longer changes. Converges in finitely many steps for finite MDPs.
detail: Policy improvement theorem guarantees monotone improvement.

q: Synchronous vs asynchronous DP?
short: Synchronous computes all new values from the previous sweep (two arrays); asynchronous updates in place in any order using the latest values, usually converging faster and allowing focus on relevant states.
example: Race car: 40 vs 49 sweeps to Δ < 0.01.

q: What is generalised policy iteration?
short: The general pattern where evaluation (make V match π) and improvement (make π greedy w.r.t. V) interact at any granularity, converging to the joint fixed point (π*, v*).
detail: Covers PI, VI, MC control, TD, actor–critic.
mistakes: Equating GPI with policy iteration only.

q: Policy iteration vs value iteration?
short: PI: full evaluation per step, explicit policy, few expensive outer iterations. VI: one max sweep per step, implicit policy, many cheap sweeps. Both converge to the optimum.

q: Derive v* for the race car.
mistakes: Forgetting to check the other actions.

q: Evaluate (slow, slow) and do one improvement.
State and justify the policy improvement theorem.
short: If q_π(s, π′(s)) ≥ v_π(s) for all s, then v_π′(s) ≥ v_π(s): expand v_π(s) ≤ q_π(s, π′(s)) = E[R + γv_π(S′)] ≤ E[R + γq_π(S′, π′(S′))] ≤ … = v_π′(s).
mistakes: Assuming improvement only at one state.

q: Why can the greedy policy be optimal before policy evaluation converges?
short: Improvement only needs the ranking of actions to be right, not exact values; in the 4×4 grid, after ~3 sweeps the action ordering already matches the optimal one.
example: Arrows fixed while values still change.

q: Why does value iteration converge?
short: The Bellman optimality operator is a γ-contraction in the max-norm, so repeated application converges to its unique fixed point v* from any start, with error shrinking by a factor γ per sweep.
mistakes: Saying it needs a good initialisation.

q: Why is DP limited in practice?
short: It needs a full model and sweeps over all states, whose number grows exponentially with state variables (curse of dimensionality). Sample-based and approximate methods relax both.
mistakes: Blaming DP for being exponential in |S|.

q: Expected vs sample updates?
short: Expected updates (DP) average over all successors using the model: exact but costly per update. Sample updates (MC, TD) use one sampled successor: cheap, need no model, but noisy.
detail: Planning in M13 can use either.
example: Race car: both successors vs one observed.
mistakes: Calling sample updates biased by definition.

q: You have a known inventory MDP with 10⁵ states. Which DP variant and why?
short: In-place value iteration or modified policy iteration with prioritised/asynchronous sweeps focusing on reachable states; vectorise backups; stop on Δ with a tolerance tied to the needed policy accuracy.
detail: Full PI evaluation may be too expensive per step.
example: Prioritise states with large Bellman error.
mistakes: Matrix inversion for evaluation at this scale.

q: Explain GPI's 'competition' between evaluation and improvement.
short: Making π greedy w.r.t. V makes V inaccurate for the new π; making V accurate for π typically makes π no longer greedy. Each step pushes toward its own goal, yet both goals coincide only at (π*, v*), so the process converges there.
detail: Geometric picture of two lines meeting.

q: How should you report convergence of DP fairly?
short: Quote the stopping rule (θ on max change), the update variant (synchronous/in-place, order) and the initial values; sweep counts differ greatly with these (race car: 49 sweeps at θ = 0.01 vs 136 at 10⁻⁶).
detail: Δ < θ doesn't bound the error to θ; error ≤ γΔ/(1 − γ).

q: How do DP, MC and TD relate in terms of GPI?
short: All follow GPI; they differ in the evaluation step: DP uses expected updates with a model and bootstraps, MC averages sampled returns without bootstrapping, TD uses sampled one-step targets and bootstraps.
detail: M5 compares them on the race car.

q: What does Q-learning have to do with value iteration?
short: Q-learning applies the Bellman optimality update for q* using one sampled transition and a step size, Q ← Q + α[r + γ maxₐ′ Q(s′, a′) − Q], i.e. a stochastic, model-free version of value iteration on action values.
